item.title: Frazier steps up to lift Indian Hill girls soccer to DIII state title
item.description: COLUMBUS, Ohio – Indian Hill’s girls soccer team relied on defense all year, but the Braves had several players who could step up and score goals when needed. In the team’s final game, it was Claire Frazier’s turn. The Indian Hill junior scored both goals for the Braves as they defeated Bay Village Bay 2-1 in the Ohio High School Athletic Association Division III girls soccer state championship game Nov. 14 at ScottsMiracle-Gro Field, the home of the Columbus Crew. Indian Hill finishes 19-0-4 and won its third state championship, first since 2018. The Braves shut out the Rockets (21-3), who had won the previous two state titles in Division III. Head coach Amy Dunlap picked up her 382nd career win. She has a 382-116-71 career record, leading the program to its eighth regional championship and now its third state title. “Just so incredibly proud of this team,” Dunlap said. “They’re resilient, they’re relentless and they just refuse to lose. And where we were when these kids came in four years ago, and then to end their senior year with the state championship, could not be any more exciting.” Frazier led the way, scoring both goals and ending the night with a team-high 11 for the season. Senior Kaylee VanDemark sparked both scoring plays. In the fifth minute, VanDemark fired a hard shot that the keeper couldn’t control. Frazier pounced on the rebound and tapped it in. In the 47th minute, VanDemark dribbled in space down the left side and crossed the ball past two opponents to Frazier, who had open space and scored from about eight yards out. “I know Claire’s always going to put her body on the line for the team,” VanDemark said. “She works really hard. Her dedication is unmatchable. I knew I could take (my) player on, so I took her on. I knew (Claire) was going to finish it because she puts everything on the line out there. It was amazing and I was so proud of her." Frazier is one of six players with five goals or more for the Braves. She was in the best form of the group this week, scoring one of the team’s goals in the state semifinals, a 2-1 win over Bexley. Senior Allie McCauley had the other and was second on the team with nine goals. They didn’t get many chances against a Rockets defense that conceded only 16 goals coming in, but they made them count. Indian Hill had 10 shots, six on goal. “I think they’re well-disciplined,” Bay head coach Scott Simpson said. “They play well. They play on the back well. They were calm and composed. Technically I thought they were pretty solid. They didn't have a lot of bad touches. That's one of the triggers you have for pressing things if you take bad touches and lose possession. I thought they were pretty consistent there.” The Braves nearly shut out a Rockets team that had scored 106 goals for the season and had five players in double figures. item.title: Pulisic Scores Twice As USMNT Crushes Haiti 6-0
item.description: Credit: David Santiago-Imagn Images Christian Pulisic scored two goals in just two minutes to push the United States men’s national team to a dominant 6-0 victory over Haiti on Saturday night. The win came in Miami during the first leg of the Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals, marking the biggest rout of Mauricio Pochettino’s two years leading the squad. This result sets up a formality for the return leg in Cincinnati on Tuesday, where the current coach will take charge for the very last time. The buildup to this series carried heavy weight because Pochettino is leaving after only three months of a new four-year contract to become the manager of Manchester United, according to ESPN . Players showed no signs of distraction despite the looming change in leadership. Auston Trusty, who scored the opening goal from a corner kick in the 10th minute, spoke to TNT about the team’s focus on their departing coach. “We played for him,” Trusty told TNT. “Obviously he’s our gaffer. Obviously it’s sad that he’s moving on. Obviously it’s a great opportunity that he is moving on into, but we play for him. It’s his team, it’s his identity.” Trusty also noted that the mindset remains to win every single game and keep fighting no matter how large the lead becomes. Pulisic returned to action for the first time since suffering an injury during a round-of-16 exit at the World Cup. Fourth on the team’s all-time leading scorers list, he surpassed Eric Wynalda thanks to his two second-half strikes. Five goals followed in a one-sided second half, with Weston McKennie and Folarin Balogun rounding out the scoring alongside a fourth goal from teenager Julian Hall. Hall netted his fourth goal in just five appearances, a game that officially cap-tied him to the U.S. after he was previously eligible to represent Poland. A Final Sendoff in Miami Haiti was technically the home team for Saturday match, but the fixture moved to Miami due to ongoing gang violence in the Caribbean nation. The U.S. players executed a plan that left the opposition with little chance to respond, proving that the team can perform at a high level even when the coaching future remains uncertain. Next March, the Nations League semifinals and final are set to occur, with the U.S. under a yet-to-be-named new coach. While the team celebrates this massive win, attention shifts quickly to the search for the next leader. The United States Soccer Federation is reportedly pursuing Pep Guardiola aggressively, as initial negotiations are anticipated to begin next week. Since resigning as Manchester City’s manager in May 2026, Guardiola has been a highly-coveted free agent after securing 41 trophies over his 19 years managing in Europe. He reportedly turned down an offer of $11 million per season from Italy to take a year off. item.title: Lincoln Riley drives USC insane with another loss. It's time to pull plug | Opinion
item.description: What's the defintion of insanity? Well, it's Southern California. Because the Trojans keep doing the same thing over and over, expecting different results. In a result that has become an annual tradition, No. 14 USC lost another ranked game in November that has spoiled its hopes of the College Football Playoff . The 2026 edition of coach Lincoln Riley's tenure featured another mistake-riddled affair, blowing it against Indiana in a 27-13 loss . Riley is now just 6-15 in ranked games with the Trojans, including 1-9 on the road with the lone victory coming in his first season in 2022. Feeling insane yet? No matter how much talent he acquires or how the table is set perfectly for him, Riley continuously falls short in the games he not only is expected to win, but has to. No one cares he is 36-6 when facing unranked teams. When you're at USC, you're supposed to win the big games, and when you don't, that's when it's time for the bags to start being packed. USC was facing an Indiana team that hasn't been able to move the ball for over a month, and let backup quarterback Grant Wilson − making his first start since he was at Old Dominion in 2024 − throw for 305 yards and two touchdowns, opening up a battle at quarterback for the Hoosiers. It was the most points Indiana had scored since early October. Indiana has one of the best defenses in the country, but the loaded Trojans offense was meant to break it down just like how it did against Ohio State. Instead, USC was limited to just 13 points, and with Jayden Maiava throwing a season-high three interceptions, including in the red zone as the Trojans were on the cusp of tying the game late in the fourth quarter. USC also had both of its kickers miss a field goal. Once again, Riley's team completely implodes when the light at brightest. USC earned some credit back when it beat Ohio State on Halloween night , but that wasn't the end of it. Riley had to finally prove he could win those battles on the road, and instead he lost his eighth in a row. What may drive you even crazier is how after each defeat, Riley insists his team was "this close" to winning, forgetting being close only counts in horseshoes and hand grenades. However, a hand grenade just went off on USC's season. While not mathematically out of it just yet, 7-3 USC can kiss its CFP hopes goodbye just like its done every season under its coach, still yet to make the field since the playoff's inception in 2014. After consistently falling short, maybe that's why Riley was vocal about his desire to expand it to 24-teams, that way he can finally feel a sense of validation when he's able to win eight or nine games in a season. item.title: How Ball State gave DePauw and Wabash another successful Monon Bell game
item.description: MUNCIE — In a game defined by the defenses, it was only fitting that the 132nd edition of the Monon Bell Classic came down to a clutch interception. With nine seconds left on the clock, Wabash quarterback Jackson Gilbert took the snap, dropped back, and launched a pass to the back left corner of the end zone for wide receiver Luke Adams. DePauw defensive back Joey Fico was there, though, and he leapt high into the air to snag the interception and seal a 16-10 victory for the Tigers at Ball State's Scheumann Stadium on Saturday, Nov. 14. "We've been practicing it all week," Fico said. "Not the pick, but the coverages. We knew that (Adams) was their guy, we got into a deep-third coverage, I saw him lined up one-on-one across from me. Their guy on our guy, I knew the ball was going to come up, and I was like, 'It's got to be me.' "I got up, did what I did, and the rest is history." As Fico came crashing down to the turf, the raucous crowd of DePauw fans and students that had filled up Ball State's bleachers erupted with thunderous cheers as the Tigers clinched their fifth-straight win over their archrival Little Giants. "You can't go to any other D-III school like Wabash and DePauw and get the support you get," Fico said. "I want to say a big thanks to all my friends and family that showed up because it does mean something. I definitely do play harder when there's a bunch of people out in front, knowing that they're supporting me." The Monon Bell Classic is not just the best Division III college football rivalry. It is considered by many to be the greatest rivalry the sport has to offer, no matter what level, and is one of the most historic rivalries in all of American sports, dating all the way back to 1890. With the two schools located just 27 miles apart in western Indiana — Wabash in Crawfordsville and DePauw in Greencastle — the rivaling rosters are often composed of high school teammates or even relatives. More: DePauw outlasts Wabash in 132nd Monon Bell game | Final score, highlights The Monon Bell itself — a 300-pound locomotive bell taken from the Monon Railroad — was introduced as a traveling trophy in 1932 and has famously been stolen by students from each school on nine different occasions. The famous Bell made its way through the procession of DePauw tailgaters that flooded the Scheumann Stadium parking lot before the game, and DePauw staffers and students rang it loudly and proudly before, during and after the game. How Ball State became the host for the 2026 Monon Bell Classic From 1915 until 1922, the rivalry game was held at neutral sites to accommodate larger crowds and alumni. The 1922 meeting at Irwin Field in Indianapolis marked the last time that the game was played at a neutral site until this year's meeting at Ball State. DePauw was set to host this year, but the school is currently undergoing a massive stadium renovation project that forced the administration to seek out neutral site options. item.title: Japan can be world's best, says outgoing coach Moriyasu
item.description: Japan beat Brazil 3-2 in a firendly in Singapore on Saturday (Roslan RAHMAN) Coach Hajime Moriyasu said Japan can become the best in the world after beating Brazil for a second time, as he prepares to step down after eight years in charge. Japan shocked the five-times world champions 3-2 in a friendly in Singapore on Saturday, with substitute Tatsuhiro Sakamoto scoring an injury-time winner. The victory came just more than a year after Japan beat Brazil for the first time in a friendly in Tokyo. Brazil eliminated Japan from this year's World Cup in North America with a 2-1 win in the last 32. Moriyasu will leave his job after a friendly against Paraguay on Tuesday but he is certain that Japan are on track to become a major football nation. "The players showed confidence and courage and dug in when they needed to dig in," he said. "At the World Cup in the future, Japan can absolutely become the world's best." Moriyasu, Japan's longest-serving coach, was originally set to lead the team at the Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia in January before handing the reins to current Under-23 boss Go Oiwa. But the Asian Football Confederation announced that the tournament would be pushed back to December 2027 due to "exceptional circumstances" in the region, following Houthi attacks on the host country. The JFA confirmed on Friday that next week's game would be Moriyasu's last. "Aiming for wins and growth, I will strive to do my best as I always have," Moriyasu said. Japan were looking for revenge after a heart-breaking loss to Brazil at the World Cup. Gabriel Martinelli scored in the 95th minute in Houston to send Brazil through. Japan midfielder Ao Tanaka, who was in floods of tears after making a late mistake in the World Cup game, said after the win in Singapore that he was "calm but really happy". "All sorts of things started coming back to me as the game got closer, and of course those frustrating memories were in my head," said the Leeds United midfielder. Japan took an early 2-0 lead before Brazil hit back through two Vinicius Junior wonder strikes. Coventry winger Sakamoto won it for Japan in injury time, before Brazil coach Carlo Ancelotti and captain Raphinha were sent off for protesting the goal. The 30-year-old Sakamoto was making his first Japan appearance for five years. "To come back like this and make a contribution in such a massive match, one we all really wanted to win, gives me so much confidence," said Sakamoto. amk/tc

item.description: USMNT deliver six-goal statement in Mauricio Pochettino's penultimate match By Ari Liljenwall Mauricio Pochettino's tenure with the US men's national team is nearing its conclusion, but he's making sure it ends with a flourish. With their head coach set to depart for Manchester United following Tuesday's second leg, the USMNT delivered a comprehensive performance on Saturday, dismantling Haiti 6-0 at Inter Miami 's Nu Stadium in the opening match of their Concacaf Nations League quarterfinal. Christian Pulisic struck twice, while Auston Trusty, Julian Hall , Weston McKennie and Folarin Balogun also found the scoresheet as the USMNT turned a narrow halftime advantage into a rout, putting one foot in the Nations League semifinals. Final flourish The result came amid an unusual backdrop, as the team entered Saturday's match facing considerable uncertainty following the news of Pochettino's impending departure. The Argentine's decision to leave for Manchester United sent shockwaves through the program, coming just months after he signed a contract extension following the 2026 FIFA World Cup . Instead of building toward another cycle under Pochettino, the USMNT suddenly found themselves preparing for another coaching transition. But if the news threatened to become a distraction, it hardly showed on the field. The Yanks put the uncertainty aside and delivered one of the most dominant performances of Pochettino's tenure, giving their outgoing manager plenty to celebrate as he approaches his final match in charge. Rising star, established star Among the biggest individual standouts was the 18-year-old Hall, who continued his rapid ascent with another milestone moment on the international stage. The Manhattan native has enjoyed a breakout 2026 campaign with Red Bull New York , recording 13g/5a in 33 MLS appearances. He also became the youngest player in league history to net a hat trick and earned his first MLS All-Star selection. On Saturday, he scored his fourth international goal in five games with a composed finish in transition, adding another highlight to his burgeoning USMNT career and showcasing his growing importance to the program's next generation. Meanwhile, Christian Pulisic reminded everyone of his enduring value in his first match back with the squad since this summer's World Cup. The long-time US star delivered a brace that included a penalty kick and a spectacular individual strike from outside the penalty box. The AC Milan star's performance underscored the attacking quality at Pochettino's disposal, with nine separate players tallying a goal contribution on the evening. Last dance With a commanding six-goal advantage heading into Tuesday's return leg at FC Cincinnati 's TQL Stadium, the US are firmly in control of their Nations League quarterfinal tie. item.title: Lindy Duncan takes 1-shot lead into final round of The Annika
item.description: The Annika leader Lindy Duncan, right, hugs Carlota Ciganda at the 18th hole following Saturday's third round. The two started the day in a three-way tie for the lead, but Ciganda slipped six strokes behind. ©Luis Santana Lindy Duncan entered Saturday sharing the lead at The Annika. By the end of the third round, she had slightly separated herself from the field, moving one step closer to her first LPGA Tour victory. Duncan shot a bogey-free 1-under 69 at Pelican Golf Club in Belleair to reach 13 under through 54 holes, taking a one-stroke lead over Hye-Jin Choi into Sunday’s final round. With cooler temperatures and gusty winds making scoring difficult, Duncan relied on steady play, recording 17 pars and one birdie to maintain her position atop the leaderboard. “So far, the first two days was kind of low scoring, and (Saturday) was a really tough day with the wind,” said Duncan, who was born in Fort Lauderdale and grew up in Plantation. “The greens firmed up, so it was really just trying to hit the ball in spots where you could at least hit the green or have a reasonable chip.” After making nine consecutive pars on the front nine, Duncan broke through with a birdie on the par-4 11th hole. She hit a 7-iron onto the green, leaving herself an approximately 18- to 20-foot putt that she converted into her only birdie of the day. Lindy Duncan tees off on the No. 8 hole. The Florida native, seeking her first LPGA Tour victory, shoots 1-under 69 to take a one-shot lead into the final round. Duncan closed with seven consecutive pars, including a challenging finish on the 18th hole. Facing a 192-yard approach into the wind, she was concerned about carrying the ball far enough to clear the water guarding the green. Her shot barely cleared the hazard, leaving her with an opportunity to save par. “I was a little bit low on the face and it was low, like, the flight of it, so I was pretty concerned that it — I didn’t think it was going to clear, and I don’t think it cleared by very much,” Duncan said. She followed with a par-saving putt to preserve her bogey-free round. Choi, who began the day tied for the lead with Duncan and Carlota Ciganda, shot even-par 70 to remain at 12 under. item.title: Amateurs Waste Strokes On Seven Short-Game Myths
item.description: USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect Many golfers spend hours perfecting their full swing only to lose shots around the green due to outdated advice. A fresh analysis from MyGolfSpy breaks down seven specific myths that keep handicaps high. The report, updated for 2026, targets fundamental errors in bunker play, chipping, and wedge selection that plague amateurs from 35 to 65. These aren’t just minor tweaks; they are fundamental misconceptions that turn distance and spin into guesswork for players trying to lower their scores. The instruction industry has long passed down rules that don’t match how the game is actually played on tour. MyGolfSpy points out that players often exaggerate these techniques, leading to poor contact and low spin rates. The data suggests that sticking to rigid rules without understanding the physics of the clubface leads to costly mistakes. Golfers need to stop believing that one stance or one grip works for every lie around the green. The Bunker Stance Trap The first major myth involves the bunker setup. Many amateurs are told to “Open your stance in the bunker and swing along your feet.” MyGolfSpy notes that while an open stance is valid, exaggerating it causes the handle to drift ahead of the clubhead. This de-lofts the club, sending the ball out low with little spin. Tour players often use a more square setup to let the bounce work properly. If a player keeps the stance too open, the ball comes out uncontrollable. Aim more square to allow the clubhead to release toward the target. For long bunker shots, the advice to square a 60-degree wedge to make it go farther is also flawed. MyGolfSpy states, “For long bunker shots, square a 60-degree wedge to make it go farther.” This is a trap because a 52 or 54-degree wedge with an open face actually beats a squared 60-degree wedge for distance and control. Plugged Lies and Wrist Locks When the ball sits deep in the sand, the instinct to “Plugged lie? Close the face and chop it out” is dangerous. A plugged lie with a closed face launches the ball hot and uncontrollable. The report warns that this technique fails because the club cannot slide under the ball effectively. Another persistent myth claims players “Don’t use your wrists in the short game.” MyGolfSpy explains that the myth exists because many players have overactive wrists, but locking them up creates problems. The source explicitly states, “Locking your wrists in the short game turns distance and spin into guesswork.” A gentle hinge on the way back and a soft release through are far better for consistency. Trying to hit the ball with a stiff wrist removes the necessary feel for the shot. Thick Rough and Chip Weight Thick rough often leads golfers to believe they should “In thick rough, play it back and hit down hard.” MyGolfSpy advises against this aggressive approach. item.title: Ryan Conwell Proves Heat Found Gold In Second-Round Pick
item.description: Credit: Cary Edmondson-Imagn Images Ryan Conwell just dropped 20 points on the Cleveland Cavaliers, and that performance changes the whole conversation about Miami’s backcourt. This rookie is not just filling time; he is making plays when the team needs them most. Sun Sentinel ‘s Ira Winderman notes that Conwell has emerged as a valuable second-round selection for the franchise. The numbers back up the hype from Friday night. Conwell finished with five rebounds while shooting 6-for-12 from the field and 4-for-9 from deep against the Cavs, per All U Can Heat . His last four games show a player on the rise, averaging 11 points and hitting 40 percent of his threes. The Heat went 3-1 during this specific stretch, proving the rookie’s impact on the win column. A Scorer When Others Are Out Heat fans know how thin the roster gets when injuries pile up. Pelle Larsson and Klay Thompson sat out the Friday night victory, leaving a massive hole in the lineup. Conwell stepped in and logged 33 minutes, playing more than any Heat player aside from Bam Adebayo and Davion Mitchell, according to All U Can Heat. That heavy workload shows exactly how much the coaching staff trusts him right now. But there is a clear difference between Conwell and other options. Sun Sentinel reporter Ira Winderman noted that comparing Conwell to Kasparas Jakucionis is somewhat apples to oranges. Jakucionis is more of a point guard, while Conwell operates as an undersized scorer who can create his own shot. This distinction matters because Miami needs someone who can score when the defense collapses. Depth Issues Still Loom Large Even with a strong showing, the team faces a tough reality about its backcourt. Ira Winderman highlighted that insufficient depth at the point guard spot continues to be a major concern for Miami. During Friday’s matchup, Erik Spoelstra faced significant difficulty resting Davion Mitchell, while Dru Smith contributed little in his short appearance. The truth is that the Heat likely require point guard depth more than in any other area. The story of how Conwell landed in Miami adds another layer to his value. Per Sun Sentinel, he resulted from a compensatory second-round pick the Heat obtained from the Hornets because they were not informed about the gambling investigation depth concerning Terry Rozier before the trade. That pick turned into a player who arrived exactly when needed. Some fans might compare his future value to the first-round pick the Hornets still hold from the Rozier trade, which is top-14 protected in June and otherwise unprotected in 2028, according to reports. That potential future asset highlights just how valuable a current contributor like Conwell can be. A more fitting comparison for Ryan could be whatever asset the Hornets eventually acquire from that first-round selection.
